summary:
Earth Trend Detective turns NASA Earth-science data into plain answers to the challenge’s four questions: what is changing, where, how much, and is it significant? Pick one of six variables (precipitation, solar radiation, soil moisture, surface runoff, nitrogen dioxide, ozone) and see a trend map of the whole Americas (669 states, provinces and departments in 49 countries), then a 1984–2025 time series with the rate of change per decade and an honest verdict: rising, falling or “no clear trend”. 
Verdicts use the Mann-Kendall test and Sen slope, corrected for seasonality, autocorrelation and multiple comparisons. 
A detective game with random questions and real stories teaches students and the public how to read trends. 
It is bilingual (English and Spanish), accessible (WCAG 2.2 AA automated checks) and open source.
details:
What it does: The Explorer shows a state-level trend map, a time series you can brush to choose years, and a verdict card. Filters change the zone (continent, sub-continents, desert, rainforest, estuary, large city), detail (annual or monthly) and years analysed. Scientific mode adds the Sen-slope confidence interval, Mann-Kendall Z, t, R², lag-1 autocorrelation and the test used. “My place” shows all variables for one location. The Detective challenge draws six random questions per round from banks of data cases, statistics concepts and 8 true stories.

How it works : Monthly values on a 1° grid are averaged per state, the seasonal cycle is removed, and a Mann-Kendall test and Sen slope give the rate per decade, with an OLS t-test and 95% CI as a second opinion. If neighbouring years are correlated the test switches to trend-free pre-whitening. Because 669 states are tested at once, p-values get a Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction. With under 10 years or over 30% missing data it answers “not enough data”, and p ≥ 0.05 is “no clear trend”, never “no change”. 22 automated tests check the statistics (false-alarm rate on noise, power on real trends, autocorrelated noise, agreement with scipy).

Impact: It is a teaching and exploration tool for high-school and university students and the public, as the challenge suggests: plain definitions of each variable, demonstration cases, and a glossary.

Creativity: A continent-wide state map with country-colored selection, a game built from real stories and random questions, a map that centers on your country, and results that admit uncertainty.

Tools: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind, MapLibre GL, Plotly (web); FastAPI, xarray, scipy, pymannkendall, statsmodels, shapely (API); Docker and Render for hosting.

Honest limits: Soil moisture and ozone come from the MERRA-2 reanalysis through NASA POWER, not from GLDAS and OMI. Surface runoff and NO₂ are clearly labelled demonstration layers: reading real GLDAS records was tested but not completed in time. Trends are linear and the grid is 1° (~110 km).
